info: One correction to my earlier advice

I overstated the tap-water issue. Extension sources do agree that corn plants and Janet Craig types are very sensitive to fluoride, and that it accumulates in the leaves gradually over time. But one horticulturist points out that the standard 0.7 ppm level in city water is below the roughly 1.0 ppm that damages sensitive plants, and that's EBMUD's level. So filtered water is a cheap precaution, not a must. Letting the soil dry too much between waterings, especially combined with over-fertilizing, also causes brown tips. 
Dracaena-Tip Burn | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks +2

New plan: all three plants, Berkeley seasons
	Corn plant (floor)	Marginata	Janet Craig (small)
Water when	Top ~half of soil dry	Top ~half dry	Top ~half dry
Spring/Summer	~every 10–14 days	~every 7–10 days	~every 7–10 days
Fall	~every 2–3 wks	~every 10–14 days	~every 10–14 days
Winter	~every 3–4 wks	~every 2–3 wks	~every 2–3 wks
Light	Bright indirect	Brightest of the three	Tolerates the lowest light
Watering method: Check with a finger or chopstick, since the intervals are only estimates. Water until it drains, then empty any standing water. The big pot sits on a fabric mat with no saucer, so a saucer is worth adding. Overwatering is the most common way to kill all three.
Fertilizer: Half-strength liquid houseplant food, about monthly from April to August. None from September to March. Too much fertilizer causes tip burn.
Temperature: Keep all three above 55°F and away from the radiator's direct heat. The corn plant is closest, so move it a couple of feet over before heating season.
Monthly: Wipe dust off the leaves, rotate each pot a quarter turn, and look under leaves for spider mites, especially in winter.
Leaf cleanup: Trim brown tips with clean scissors along the leaf's natural shape. Pull off fully dry lower leaves on the marginata; that shedding is normal.
Repotting: Not this year. IKEA says repotting isn't needed until a year after purchase. Next spring at the earliest. 
IKEA

If you do the flex test on the big plant and the leaf actually snaps or pokes, tell me and I'll switch that plant to a yucca plan: more direct sun and much drier soil.

What kind of fertilizer

Any balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer, diluted to half strength. Specifics:

Best ratio: roughly 3-1-2 (N-P-K), which matches what foliage plants actually use. Dyna-Gro Foliage-Pro 9-3-6 is the common pick and includes the micronutrients most cheap fertilizers skip.

And I need to get a nice looking pot for the large plant so what should I get there?
It’s the ikea tropisk plant
Do some Research and find the best option to get on Amazon for cheap for fertilizer
Pot: don't repot, just slip it into a cachepot.
The TROPISK is in a 12" nursery pot and doesn't need repotting for about a year after purchase.
A decorative outer pot lets you keep the nursery pot's drainage and just lift the plant out over the sink to water.
What to look for:
Inner diameter 13–14" so the 12" nursery pot slides in and out easily
Height 11–12" so the black rim hides but the pot doesn't swallow the trunk
A wide, heavy base.
Your plant is about 4.5 ft and top-heavy.
Ceramic, stoneware, or fiberclay resists tipping; thin lightweight plastic doesn't.
No drainage hole needed in a cachepot.
Just pour out anything that collects, or drop a shallow saucer inside.
Cheapest good option: IKEA Emeryville is minutes from you and sells 12"–14" cachepots for a fraction of Amazon prices, and you can eyeball the fit against the pot you already own.
On Amazon, search "14 inch cachepot indoor" and filter to ceramic or fiberclay.
Typical fiberclay floor planters in that size run roughly $35–60.
Fertilizer: I can't see live Amazon prices, so I can't rank by actual cost right now.
What I can tell you is which product fits:
Dyna-Gro Foliage-Pro 9-3-6, 8 oz is the one to get.

It's a complete formula with all 6 macronutrients and all 10 micronutrients, and its N-P-K ratio is also suited to phosphorus-sensitive plants — which matters for dracaenas, since superphosphate is a fluoride source.
It's urea-free, which limits salt buildup, and needs only ¼ tsp per gallon, so an 8 oz bottle will outlast these three plants by years.
DYNA-GRO FOLIAGE-PRO™ 9-3-6 - 8 oz | GHViolets +2
Budget alternative: any generic 20-20-20 or Miracle-Gro Indoor Plant Food, used at half strength.
It works, it's cheaper up front, but it lacks the micronutrients and carries more salt.
Given the ¼ tsp per gallon dose, Foliage-Pro is the cheaper option per use even if the bottle costs more.

How do I apply fertilizer
Mix it into water, then water normally.
Never apply to dry soil or pour it straight on the roots.
Water first if the soil is bone dry.
Plain water, wait an hour.
Fertilizer on dry roots burns them.
Mix in a jug.
Foliage-Pro is ¼ tsp per gallon at full strength, so use about ⅛ tsp per gallon for these three, or roughly a drop or two per quart.
Shake it up.
Pour slowly over the whole soil surface, not down one side, until a little runs out the bottom.
Dump the runoff.
Don't let any pot sit in it.
Keep it off the leaves, especially out of the crown where the corn plant's leaves meet the cane.
Water pooling there causes rot.
Amounts per watering: roughly a half gallon for the big pot, a cup or so for each small one.
Timing: do this on a normal watering day, about once a month from April through August.
Skip it September through March.
If you ever doubt whether you fed it, skip.
Under-fertilizing a dracaena is harmless; over-fertilizing shows up as burnt leaf tips.
